questions.q: A heron wades in a village pond that also holds fish. According to the chapter, where do the fish and the heron get the oxygen they need?
questions.a: The fish takes oxygen from the water and the heron from the air
o: The fish takes oxygen from the water and the heron from the air
Both take their oxygen from the water of the pond
Both take their oxygen from the soil at the pond's edge
The fish takes oxygen from the air and the heron from water

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A fish kept in clean, oxygen-rich water but given no food at all will not survive for long.
Reason (R): A fish obtains its biotic needs, such as food, from small plants and animals in its habitat.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true

questions.q: Hira claims: 'The bark of a single tree can be a habitat, and everything an organism takes from its habitat is living.' Is her claim right, wrong or partly right? Explain, using a pond fish as your example.
questions.a: Partly right. The first part is right: a habitat is the place where an organism lives and it can be as small as the bark of a tree. The second part is wrong: a habitat gives abiotic needs as well as biotic ones. A pond fish gets food (biotic) from small plants and animals, but it gets oxygen (abiotic) from the water, so its needs are not all living.
s: Verdict: partly right
Right part: a habitat can be as small as tree bark
Wrong part: abiotic needs such as oxygen from water also come from the habitat

questions.q: A student's list of the components of a pond has 4 biotic and 3 abiotic entries. Write a list for a pond that fits this, and then say how many more abiotic entries the chapter's own list of abiotic components (air, water, soil, sunlight and temperature) would add if your list shows only water and soil and one other.
questions.a: Sample answer. Biotic: fish, frogs, lotus, algae. Abiotic: water, soil, sunlight. The chapter's list has five abiotic components (air, water, soil, sunlight, temperature); the sample shows three, so two more (air and temperature) would complete it. Any list of four living and three non-living pond components with a correct count of the missing abiotic ones earns the marks.
s: Four correct biotic pond components
Three correct abiotic pond components
Counts the missing abiotic components of the chapter's five (here 2)

questions.q:
A school in Bhopal has a small pond with fish. The school raised the daily fish food every month, but the fish kept dying (illustrative record).
Month | Fish food per day (g) | Water depth (cm) | Pond surface with water plants (%) | Fish counted
March | 100 | 120 | 60 | 50
April | 150 | 80 | 30 | 31
May | 200 | 40 | 10 | 18
(a) Name the four conditions a pond provides that are essential for the fish to survive.
(b) Which conditions does the record show getting worse?
(c) What percentage of the March fish were still alive in May?
(d) Plan 1 is to double the daily food again, which can be started tomorrow. Plan 2 is to keep the pond topped up with water and replant water plants, which takes a few weeks. Which plan will save more fish? Justify using the record.
questions.a: (a) Food, oxygen, shelter and space to grow. (b) Space and oxygen-giving water are shrinking (depth fell from 120 to 40 cm), and the water plants, which give shelter and release oxygen, fell from 60% to 10%. (c) 18 / 50 x 100 = 36%. (d) Plan 2. Food rose from 100 g to 200 g a day, yet the fish fell from 50 to 18, so food was not what ran short. What fell were water, space, shelter and plants, so restoring water and water plants deals with the needs that the record shows were failing.
s: Part (a): food, oxygen, shelter, space to grow
Part (b): water depth (space) and water plants (shelter, oxygen) falling
Part (c): 36%
Part (d): Plan 2; food stayed the same, so the shortage is water, space and plants

questions.q:
A deer drinks at a forest waterhole and grazes on grass and the leaves of plants. A student says: 'If a pond holds plenty of food for its fish, a forest deer could live in it too.'
(a) Test the claim: what does the deer need from its habitat that the pond cannot give?
(b) What does this show about different habitats?
questions.a: (a) The deer feeds only on plants (grass and leaves) and lives on land; a pond does not offer these living conditions, however much food the fish have. (b) Every organism needs specific conditions to survive, and different habitats offer different living conditions, so each organism lives where its own needs are met.
s: Part (a): the deer needs plant food and land conditions that the pond lacks
Part (b): each organism needs specific conditions; habitats differ

questions.q:
A village panchayat near a forest in Odisha kept this record (illustrative figures).
Year | Forest cover in the nearby block (sq km) | Waterholes still holding water in May | Elephant visits to the village
2019 | 52 | 9 | 3
2021 | 47 | 6 | 7
2023 | 41 | 3 | 15
The panchayat can afford only one of two plans. Plan 1: a solar fence around the village fields, ready in two months, which keeps elephants out of the fenced fields. Plan 2: working with the forest department to restore the corridor to a larger forest 8 km away, which will take about three years.
(a) Which two columns show the change in the elephants' habitat, and what does each show?
(b) Using the chapter, explain why these changes lead to more visits.
(c) How many times as many visits were there in 2023 as in 2019, and about how many times did the visits multiply every two years?
(d) Choose the plan that will do more for the village over the next ten years. Justify using the record.
questions.a: (a) Forest cover (52, 47, 41 sq km) shows the forest shrinking; waterholes holding water (9, 6, 3) show water drying up. (b) With less forest and fewer waterholes, the elephants' habitat has too little food and water, and with their habitat lost they move into human habitats in search of food. (c) 15 / 3 = 5 times; the visits roughly doubled every two years (3 to 7 to 15). (d) Plan 2. The fence gives quick protection, but the record shows the habitat is still shrinking every year, so hungry elephants would keep coming and press on the fence or move to the next village. Restoring the corridor lets them reach a larger forest with food and water, which deals with the cause shown in the record, so over ten years it does more even though it is slower.
s: Part (a): forest cover shrinking and waterholes drying
Part (b): habitat loss leaves too little food and water, so elephants enter human areas
Part (c): 5 times; roughly doubling every two years
Part (d): Plan 2, as the habitat keeps shrinking and only the corridor gives access to food and water

questions.q: True or False? 'The abiotic components of a habitat are only the things we can touch, such as soil and water; sunlight and temperature are not components of a habitat.' Give the verdict and the correction.
questions.a: False. The abiotic components are all the non-living things of a habitat: air, water, soil, sunlight and temperature. Sunlight and temperature are abiotic components even though they cannot be touched, and they can change between day and night in the same habitat.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: sunlight and temperature are abiotic components too (air, water, soil, sunlight, temperature)

questions.q: Compare a pond habitat and a forest habitat on five points: (1) two biotic components of each, (2) two abiotic components of each, (3) where a typical animal of each gets its oxygen, (4) one way the conditions in each can vary within the habitat, (5) what the two habitats have in common.
questions.a: (1) Pond: fish, frogs, lotus, algae (any two). Forest: grass, trees, birds (any two). (2) Pond: water, soil. Forest: soil, air (or sunlight). (3) A fish takes oxygen from the water; a forest animal takes oxygen from the air. (4) A forest can be warm by day and cool at night, so day-active and night-active animals face different conditions; physical conditions such as sunlight and temperature also vary in a pond. (5) Both have biotic and abiotic components that interact, though the kinds of living and non-living things differ.
s: (1) two biotic components of each
(2) two abiotic components of each
(3) oxygen from water for a fish, from air for a forest animal
(4) variation within a habitat (day and night temperature)
(5) both have biotic and abiotic components that interact

questions.q: A student lists what she saw in one forest: deer, soil, sal tree, sunlight, mushroom, air, temperature, snake, grass and bacteria in the soil. Analyse the list in five points: (1) how many biotic and how many abiotic components, (2) the ratio of biotic to abiotic in simplest form, (3) how many are animals, how many plants and how many fungi or microbes, (4) which listed abiotic component changes between day and night and so makes a snake active at night and a rodent active by day face different conditions, (5) why the same list could not be used for a pond.
questions.a: (1) Biotic: deer, sal tree, mushroom, snake, grass, bacteria = 6; abiotic: soil, sunlight, air, temperature = 4. (2) 6 : 4 = 3 : 2. (3) Animals: deer and snake = 2; plants: sal tree and grass = 2; fungi or microbes: mushroom and bacteria = 2. (4) Temperature (and the sunlight that goes with it): a forest is warm by day and cool at night, so a night-active snake and a day-active rodent meet different conditions in the same habitat. (5) A pond has different living beings and different non-living things, since different habitats offer different living conditions; its list would hold fish, lotus and water, for example.
s: (1) 6 biotic, 4 abiotic
(2) ratio 3 : 2
(3) 2 animals, 2 plants, 2 fungi or microbes
(4) temperature differs between day and night, so conditions differ
(5) a pond has different components, as habitats differ

questions.q:
With their teacher, students took readings at noon at three spots in one school garden (illustrative).
Spot | Soil | Temperature (degrees C) | Light
Under a dense neem tree | moist | 26 | dim
Open lawn | dry | 34 | bright
Beside the water tank | wet | 28 | medium
(a) Name two abiotic components that differ from spot to spot.
(b) What is the difference between the warmest and the coolest spot?
(c) Earthworms were found only under the neem tree and beside the tank. Use the readings and the chapter to explain why.
questions.a: (a) Any two of soil moisture, temperature and light. (b) 34 - 26 = 8 degrees C. (c) Earthworms live in moist soil; only the spots under the tree and beside the tank have moist or wet soil, while the open lawn is dry and hot. Physical conditions vary within one habitat, so organisms live in the parts that meet their needs.
s: Part (a): two of soil moisture, temperature, light
Part (b): 8 degrees C
Part (c): earthworms need moist soil, found only at those spots

questions.q: On a class visit to a pond with his teacher, Sameer lists what he saw: fish, frogs, lotus, water, soil, algae, dragonflies and sunlight. The number of abiotic components in his list is ___.

Riya says the bark of the old neem tree in her school is far too small to count as a habitat. Her friend points out something they observed on the bark. Which observation best shows that Riya is wrong?
questions.a: Ants and a spider live and feed on the bark
o: Ants and a spider live and feed on the bark
The bark is part of a living tree, so it is biotic
The bark is warmed by sunlight and wetted by rain
The neem tree is taller than the school building

questions.q:
Read these statements about habitats.
Statement 1: A pond and a forest both have biotic and abiotic components, though the kinds in each differ.
Statement 2: Water and soil count as biotic components of a pond, because living things depend on them.
Statement 3: Besides food and oxygen, a pond gives a fish shelter and space to grow.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: Statements 1 and 3 only
o: Statements 1 and 3 only
Statements 1 and 2 only
Statement 3 only
All three statements

questions.q:
In Table 12.3-style records of a pond, a student writes 'Many microbes are present in the pond' under biotic-abiotic interactions.
(a) Does a living thing too small to see belong with the biotic or the abiotic components?
(b) Give the reason, and name the two other groups of biotic components that the chapter lists with microbes.
questions.a: (a) Biotic. (b) The biotic components are the living beings of a habitat, and microbes are living beings even though they are tiny; the chapter lists plants and animals along with microbes as the biotic components.
s: Part (a): biotic
Part (b): microbes are living beings; plants and animals are the other groups

questions.q:
Match each observation in Column I with the idea it shows in Column II.
Column I | Column II
1. A fish takes food from small plants and oxygen from the water | a. Physical conditions vary within one habitat
2. Ferns grow in the damp shade and grass in a sunny clearing of one forest | b. Different habitats offer different living conditions
3. Fish live in the pond but never on the dry bank beside it | c. A habitat meets both biotic and abiotic needs
4. A strip of land is marked to link two forest blocks | d. Animals can move between forests without meeting people

A new highway is cut through the forest that once joined two large forest blocks, and elephants now wander into a village beside the road more often. Which step lets the elephants travel between the two forest blocks while keeping them away from homes?
questions.a: Marking a corridor that links the two forest blocks
o: Marking a corridor that links the two forest blocks
Fencing the forest edge so no animal can ever leave a block
Draining the few waterholes left inside the forest
Clearing more trees so the elephants can be seen early

questions.q:
A student fills in a table of what she saw at a pond, visited with her teacher.
Living beings: duckweed, snails, diatoms, ducks
Non-living things: water, soil, mosquito larvae, sunlight
Which entry is in the wrong column?
questions.a: Mosquito larvae
o: Mosquito larvae
Diatoms
Sunlight
Duckweed

questions.q:
(a) A forest is warm during the day and cool at night. Is this a change in a biotic or an abiotic component of the forest?
(b) Use this change to explain how a snake that comes out at night and a rodent active by day can both live in the same forest.
questions.a: (a) Abiotic: temperature is a non-living physical condition of the habitat. (b) The snake and the rodent are active at different times, so they meet different conditions (cool night, warm day) and use the forest's resources in different ways. This lets both live in the same habitat in harmony.
s: Part (a): abiotic, since temperature is a non-living condition
Part (b): active at different times, so they face different conditions and use resources differently

questions.q:
A forest block holds 12 waterholes in May of one year and only 4 two years later (illustrative).
(a) What fraction of the waterholes is left?
(b) Using the chapter, say which abiotic condition of the elephants' habitat has changed and how this could bring them to a farm.
questions.a: (a) 4 / 12 = one third. (b) Water, an abiotic component, has dried up; with food and water scarce in their habitat, elephants move into nearby farms and plantations in search of food.
s: Part (a): one third
Part (b): water (abiotic) has dried, so elephants wander to farms for food

questions.q:
A diagram of a school vegetable garden (illustrative) shows boxes linked by arrows. An arrow marked '-' means 'reduces the number of'. A direct effect is a change in something the cat itself catches; an indirect effect reaches an organism only through another organism.
Cat -> (-) -> sparrows
Sparrows -> (-) -> caterpillars
Caterpillars -> (-) -> leaves of the cabbage plants
A cat begins to visit the garden every day. Using only these arrows, work out what happens to the caterpillars and to the cabbage leaves. Show each step and say which effects of the cat are direct and which are indirect.
questions.a: Step 1: the cat reduces the sparrows. Step 2: with fewer sparrows, fewer caterpillars are eaten, so caterpillars increase. Step 3: more caterpillars reduce the cabbage leaves, so the cabbage plants lose more leaves. The effect of the cat on sparrows is direct; its effects on caterpillars and on cabbage leaves are indirect, because they pass through the sparrows (and then the caterpillars).
s: Cat reduces sparrows, so caterpillars increase
More caterpillars, so fewer cabbage leaves
Direct on sparrows; indirect on caterpillars and leaves

questions.q:
A farmer's field holds only wheat plants of one kind, sown close together (illustrative).
(a) Using the chapter, why do the wheat plants compete strongly with each other?
(b) Name one resource that may become scarce, and say what happens to the plants that get less of it.
questions.a: (a) They are all the same kind of organism, so they have the same requirements for water, nutrients (food), space and sunlight, and they all draw on the same supply. (b) Any one of water, soil nutrients, space or sunlight; plants that get less of it grow poorly, because competition leads to scarcity of resources.
s: Part (a): same kind, so the same requirements and strong competition
Part (b): a scarce resource named; plants getting less grow poorly

questions.q:
Consider these statements.
Statement 1: In the pond study, fish reduced the number of dragonflies by eating the adult dragonflies.
Statement 2: The plants, animals and microorganisms of a habitat together form its community.
Statement 3: The organisms of a community interact with and depend on one another for survival.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: Statements 2 and 3 only
o: Statements 2 and 3 only
Statements 1 and 2 only
Statement 2 only
All three statements

questions.q:
An eco-club in Nashik marked the same 1 m x 1 m patch of its garden and counted what lived there on two dates (illustrative counts).
Organism | 10 July | 10 September
Doob grass | 64 | 41
Clover | 9 | 26
Ants | 30 | 35
Earthworms | 4 | 7
(a) The club calls the 64 doob grass plants 'a population' and the four kinds of organism counted on 10 July together 'a community'. Explain why both labels are right.
(b) The patch did not change, yet the doob grass number changed. Which part of the definition of a population allows this?
(c) The club wants to write: 'Doob grass outnumbers clover in this patch.' Using numbers from both dates, decide whether this sentence is true for both dates, and say what the club should add so that the report is not misleading.
questions.a: (a) The 64 doob plants are all one kind of organism in one habitat at one time, so they form a population; the four kinds of organism together are different populations sharing the same habitat, so they form a community. (b) A population is counted at a given time; numbers change with time, so the same patch can hold a different population on another date. (c) True for both dates: 64 is more than 9, and 41 is more than 26. But the gap shrank from 64 - 9 = 55 to 41 - 26 = 15, as doob fell and clover nearly tripled, so the report should give both dates and counts rather than one number.
s: Part (a): population = one kind; community = several populations in one habitat
Part (b): a population is defined at a given time, and numbers change
Part (c): true on both dates (64 > 9, 41 > 26), but the gap fell from 55 to 15, so give both dates

questions.q: Fish eat small insect larvae in ponds. A Class 8 group wants to find out, in the way the Pond A and Pond B study did, whether fish in a pond reduce the number of mosquitoes flying around it. Plan the comparison in five points: (1) the two ponds to choose, (2) what to keep the same, (3) what to count, (4) the result that would show fish reduce mosquitoes, (5) whether the fish's effect on the mosquito larvae in the water is direct or indirect, and whether their effect on the adult mosquitoes flying around the pond is direct or indirect, with the reason. In this question a direct effect of an organism is a change in something it feeds on itself, and an indirect effect is a change that reaches another organism only through an intermediate organism. (All pond visits are to be made with a teacher.)
questions.a: (1) Two nearby ponds, one with fish and one without fish, like Pond A and Pond B. (2) Keep the ponds alike in size, depth, plants around them and the time of year, and count at the same time of day. (3) Count the mosquito larvae in the water (for example, in a fixed number of scoops) and the adult mosquitoes caught or seen in a fixed time. (4) Fewer mosquito larvae and fewer adult mosquitoes at the pond with fish would show that fish reduce mosquitoes. (5) On the larvae the effect is direct, because the fish eat the larvae themselves. On the adult mosquitoes it is indirect, because fish do not eat the flying adults; the effect reaches them only through the larvae, since fewer larvae survive to become adults.
s: (1) one pond with fish, one without
(2) other conditions kept the same
(3) count larvae and adult mosquitoes in the same way
(4) fewer larvae and fewer adult mosquitoes at the fish pond
(5) direct on larvae (eaten by fish); indirect on adults (through the larvae)

questions.q: In a 1 m x 1 m patch of a school garden, students count 20 plants of type P, 5 plants of type Q and 12 ants on the same morning. The number of different populations they have counted in the patch is ___.

A Class 8 group counts doob grass and clover in four 1 m x 1 m squares of a 30 square metre lawn on the same day (illustrative counts).
Square | Doob grass | Clover
1 | 18 | 4
2 | 22 | 6
3 | 20 | 5
4 | 16 | 5
(a) Find the average number of each plant per square metre.
(b) Their teacher says the whole lawn's population can be estimated as the average per square metre multiplied by the area. Estimate each population.
(c) A classmate counted only Square 2 and estimated the doob grass on the whole lawn from it. Find his estimate and explain why the four-square estimate is more trustworthy.
questions.a: (a) Doob: (18 + 22 + 20 + 16) / 4 = 76 / 4 = 19 per square metre. Clover: (4 + 6 + 5 + 5) / 4 = 20 / 4 = 5 per square metre. (b) Doob: 19 x 30 = 570 plants. Clover: 5 x 30 = 150 plants. (c) 22 x 30 = 660 plants, 90 more than the four-square estimate. Square 2 happened to hold the most doob grass; counts differ from place to place, so an average over several squares represents the lawn's population better than one square.
s: Part (a): averages 19 and 5 per square metre
Part (b): estimates 570 doob and 150 clover
Part (c): 660 from one square; several squares give a better picture as counts vary

questions.q:
Students from a school in Thrissur visited three village ponds with their teacher in March and kept this record (illustrative figures).
Pond | Fish | Dragonflies seen in 10 min | Bee visits to flowers in 10 min | Average seeds per plant nearby
P | many | 6 | 48 | 90
Q | few | 15 | 30 | 62
R | none | 27 | 12 | 35
(a) Which pond is most like Pond B of the chapter's study? Give the reason.
(b) Explain why the dragonfly numbers rise from P to R.
(c) How many more seeds per plant were found near P than near R, and is that more than twice as many?
(d) A student concludes: 'Fish make the plants produce seeds directly.' In this question a direct effect of an organism is a change in something it feeds on itself, and an indirect effect is a change that reaches another organism only through an intermediate organism. Using the record, decide whether this wording is correct.
questions.a: (a) Pond R: like Pond B it has no fish, the most dragonflies and the fewest seeds. (b) Fish eat dragonfly larvae; fewer fish (P to Q to R) means fewer larvae eaten, so more dragonflies. (c) 90 - 35 = 55 more seeds per plant; 90 / 35 is about 2.6, so yes, more than twice as many. (d) Not correct. The record shows the effect passes along a chain: more fish, fewer dragonflies, more bee visits, more seeds. Fish affect the dragonfly larvae directly, because they eat them; the adult dragonflies, the bee visits and the seeds are affected only indirectly, through the larvae, the dragonflies and the pollinators.
s: Part (a): Pond R, no fish, most dragonflies
Part (b): fish eat dragonfly larvae, so fewer fish means more dragonflies
Part (c): 55 more; about 2.6 times, so more than twice
Part (d): not correct; fish affect larvae directly, but seeds only indirectly through dragonflies and bees

questions.q: In the Pond A and Pond B study, take a 'direct effect' of fish to mean a change in an organism that the fish themselves eat, and an 'indirect effect' to mean a change passed on through another organism. Using these meanings, which finding is an indirect effect of fish?
questions.a: More bees and butterflies near the pond with fish
o: More bees and butterflies near the pond with fish
Fewer dragonfly larvae in the water of the pond with fish
Fewer of the small animals that fish feed on
Fish taking in their oxygen from the water of the pond

questions.q: Ravi counts 20 plants of one kind and 5 plants of another kind in one 1 m x 1 m patch of grass and says: 'All 25 plants are one population because they live in the same patch.' Is he right, wrong or partly right? Explain.
questions.a: Partly right. He is right that the plants share one habitat, the patch, at one time. He is wrong to call them one population: a population is a group of the same kind of organism, so the 20 plants form one population and the 5 plants of the other kind form a different one. Together, the different populations sharing the habitat make up a community.
s: Verdict: partly right
Right part: they share one habitat at one time
Wrong part: a population is one kind only; two kinds are two populations that form a community

questions.q: Which observation from a village pond best shows that the members of its community depend on one another?
questions.a: Ducks feed on snails that feed on duckweed
o: Ducks feed on snails that feed on duckweed
Lotus leaves float flat on the pond water
All the rohu fish swim about in one shoal
Pond water warms up quickly on summer afternoons

questions.q: A fisheries student counts the rohu in a lake (illustrative): 80 fish on 1 January and 55 fish on 1 June. Which statement fits the chapter's meaning of a population?
questions.a: The rohu population has changed, since it is counted at a given time
o: The rohu population has changed, since it is counted at a given time
The rohu population is 135, the sum of the two counts
The rohu population cannot change while the lake stays the same
Only the January fish form a population; the June fish form a community

questions.q: True or False? 'A community is just another name for a large population of one kind of organism.' Give the verdict and the correction.
questions.a: False. A population is a group of the same kind of organism in a habitat at a given time, but a community comprises the different populations that share the habitat: its plants, animals and microorganisms together.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: a community is made of different populations sharing a habitat, not one kind

questions.q: A nursery in Shimla grows a flowering plant inside a closed glasshouse. No insects, birds or bats can enter, the air inside is still, and the plants are watered only at the roots. The plants flower well but form very few fruits and seeds. Analyse this in five points: (1) the part of the flower that releases pollen, (2) the part that must receive it, (3) why few seeds form here, (4) the agents named in the chapter that are missing, (5) one change the nursery could make, with the reason.
questions.a: (1) The stamens (male parts) burst and release pollen. (2) The pollen must reach the carpels (female parts) of the same or a different flower. (3) Few seeds form because pollination, which is essential for fruits and seeds, hardly happens: nothing carries the pollen from stamens to carpels. (4) The chapter names wind, water, insects, bats and birds as carriers of pollen; in this glasshouse there is no wind, no water reaching the flowers and no insects, bats or birds. (5) The nursery could let pollinating insects in, for example by keeping a beehive inside or opening netted vents for bees, so that pollen is carried between flowers and more fruits and seeds form.
s: (1) stamens release pollen
(2) carpels must receive it
(3) little pollination, which is needed for fruits and seeds
(4) wind, water, insects, bats, birds are all missing
(5) let in pollinators such as bees, with the reason

questions.q:
In a pond community, snails feed on duckweed and ducks feed on the snails.
(a) What does this show about the members of a community?
(b) A disease kills all the snails. Explain why this affects more than just the snail population.
questions.a: (a) The organisms of a community interact with and depend on one another for survival, here for food. (b) The ducks lose a source of food, so their population can be affected, and the duckweed is no longer eaten by snails, so it can spread; a change in one population passes on to others in the community.
s: Part (a): members depend on one another (for food)
Part (b): ducks lose food and duckweed is eaten less, so other populations change

questions.q: A pond like Pond A in the chapter's study is overfished until almost no fish are left. Following the study, which change would you expect FIRST among the insects at the pond?
questions.a: More dragonflies, as fewer of their larvae are eaten
o: More dragonflies, as fewer of their larvae are eaten
Fewer dragonflies, as they depended on fish for food
More bees at once, as fish used to eat adult bees
Fewer butterflies at once, as fish used to protect them

questions.q: Before a flower bud opens, a gardener carefully removes all its petals and sepals but leaves its stamens and carpels (illustrative). Which prediction is correct?
questions.a: It can still be pollinated, as its reproductive parts remain
o: It can still be pollinated, as its reproductive parts remain
It cannot form seeds, as the petals are what make the pollen
It cannot form seeds, as the sepals are what receive the pollen
It will form seeds even if no pollen ever reaches its carpels

questions.q:
In a guava orchard (illustrative), lizards eat spiders, spiders eat flies, and flies carry pollen between guava flowers. In this question a direct effect of an organism is a change in something it feeds on itself, and an indirect effect is a change that reaches another organism only through an intermediate organism. Lizards become more numerous.
(a) Is the effect on the spiders direct or indirect, and is it an increase or a decrease?
(b) Predict the effect on the guava seeds, saying whether it is direct or indirect.
questions.a: (a) Direct, and a decrease: lizards eat spiders themselves. (b) Spiders fall, so fewer flies are eaten and flies increase; more flies carry more pollen, so more flowers are pollinated and the guava seeds increase. This effect is indirect, since it reaches the seeds only through the spiders and the flies.
s: Part (a): direct decrease in spiders
Part (b): more flies, more pollination, more seeds; indirect

questions.q:
A student sows seeds of one kind of plant in two trays of equal size (illustrative). Tray A has 20 seedlings and Tray B has 100. After four weeks the seedlings in Tray A average 24 cm and those in Tray B average 9 cm.
(a) How many centimetres taller are the average seedlings in Tray A?
(b) Use the chapter to explain the difference.
questions.a: (a) 24 - 9 = 15 cm taller. (b) All the seedlings are one kind, so they have the same requirements for water, nutrients, space and sunlight. In the crowded Tray B they compete strongly for these, so the resources become scarce for each plant and they grow less.
s: Part (a): 15 cm
Part (b): same requirements, strong competition, scarce resources

questions.q:

questions.q: A valley in Himachal Pradesh (illustrative) has a small river running past a pine forest on the slopes, a grassland and terraced farms on the lower ground. Analyse this valley in five points: (1) which of these are aquatic and which terrestrial ecosystems, (2) which one is human-made, (3) one way the river affects the farms, (4) one way the forest on the slopes can affect the soil near the river, (5) what this valley shows about ecosystems.
questions.a: (1) The river is an aquatic ecosystem; the forest, grassland and farms are terrestrial ecosystems. (2) The terraced farms are human-made. (3) The river gives water, which is essential for the crops (and all living things on the farms). (4) Tree roots hold the soil on the slopes in place and prevent erosion, so less soil is washed down towards the river. (5) The ecosystems overlap in one area and interact with each other at any given point; ecosystems can be large or small and are not sealed off from each other.
s: (1) river aquatic; forest, grassland, farms terrestrial
(2) farms human-made
(3) river water is essential for crops
(4) tree roots prevent erosion of soil
(5) ecosystems overlap and interact

questions.q: A frog lays its eggs in the shallow water at the edge of a pond. Which kind of interaction is this, and which life process does it influence?
questions.a: Biotic-abiotic; reproduction
o: Biotic-abiotic; reproduction
Among biotic components; reproduction
Biotic-abiotic; respiration
Abiotic-abiotic; nutrition

questions.q:
In a lake in Kashmir, kingfishers and otters both catch the same kind of small fish.
(a) Which kind of interaction is this: biotic-abiotic, abiotic-abiotic, or among biotic components?
(b) What does this interaction affect, and why does it matter more in a year when the small fish are few?
questions.a: (a) An interaction among biotic components (the birds and otters compete for the same fish). (b) It affects the availability of a resource needed for nutrition, the food fish. When the fish are few, the kingfishers and otters compete harder and each may get less food.
s: Part (a): among biotic components (competition for the same food)
Part (b): availability of food; with fewer fish, each gets less

questions.q: A teacher writes three labels on the board: (i) interaction between a biotic and an abiotic component; (ii) interaction between two abiotic components; (iii) interaction among biotic components. Write one situation from a paddy field that fits each label.
questions.a: Sample answer. (i) Rice plants take water from the flooded field and use sunlight to make food (or earthworms live in the wet soil). (ii) The hot sun warms the standing water of the field (or wind makes ripples on it). (iii) A frog eats insects among the rice plants (or birds and frogs compete for the same insects). Any correct situation of each kind earns the mark.

(ii) a correct abiotic-abiotic situation
(iii) a correct situation among living things

questions.q: A student makes a closed glass-jar garden (illustrative): moist soil at the bottom, small plants and moss, two snails, and the lid on. She keeps it near a sunny window. Evaluate whether it can work as a small ecosystem by explaining five points: (1) what the sunlight does, (2) what the water does, (3) what the soil does, (4) what the air inside does for the plants and the snails, (5) one way the plants change the non-living part of the jar.
questions.a: (1) Sunlight, with carbon dioxide and water, is needed by the plants to make their food. (2) Water is essential for all the living things, the plants and the snails. (3) Soil gives the plants a medium to grow in and the nutrients they need. (4) Air gives oxygen for respiration in both the plants and the snails. (5) The plants release oxygen into the air of the jar during photosynthesis (and hold moisture in the soil). Because biotic and abiotic components interact in it, the jar can work as a small ecosystem.
s: (1) sunlight for making food
(2) water essential for all organisms
(3) soil gives medium and nutrients
(4) air gives oxygen for respiration of plants and snails
(5) plants release oxygen (or keep soil moist)

questions.q: A student calls a roadside puddle that holds algae, tadpoles, mud and sunlight an ecosystem. Her friend says it is too small to be one. Who is right, going by the chapter?
questions.a: The student, since its living and non-living parts interact

questions.q: Rohan claims: 'In a pond, a single fish can take part in biotic-abiotic interactions and in interactions among biotic components, but it cannot take part in an abiotic-abiotic interaction.' Is his claim right, wrong or partly right? Explain with an example of each kind.
questions.a: Right. A fish takes part in biotic-abiotic interactions (it takes oxygen from the water, or lays its eggs in water) and in interactions among biotic components (it eats insect larvae, or is eaten by a water snake). An abiotic-abiotic interaction, such as sunlight warming the water or wind making ripples, is between two non-living components only, so the fish is not part of it.
s: Verdict: right
Fish in biotic-abiotic and biotic-biotic interactions, with an example of each
Abiotic-abiotic interactions are between non-living components only, e.g. sun warming water

questions.q: The chapter says ecosystems can be large or small. Which of these could NOT be studied as an ecosystem on its own?

Read the statements.
