questions.q:
A Class 8 group in Pune grew four bean seedlings of the same size for three weeks in a test (illustrative results).
Pot | Placed | Watered | Soil | New leaves after 3 weeks
1 | sunny window | daily | garden soil | 6
2 | dark cupboard | daily | garden soil | 0, leaves turned yellow
3 | sunny window | never | garden soil | 0, plant wilted
4 | sunny window | daily | washed sand with few nutrients | 3
(a) Which two pots should be compared to see the effect of sunlight?
(b) What does Pot 4 show about the role of soil?
(c) Pot 4 grew what fraction of the new leaves that Pot 1 grew?
(d) The school must raise seedlings for its garden in one of two places: a dark storeroom with rich garden soil and a tap for daily watering, or a sunny verandah where only sandy, poor soil is available (water can be carried to either place every day). Which place should it choose? Justify using the pots.
questions.a: (a) Pots 1 and 2: only the light differs. (b) Soil provides nutrients for plant growth; in nutrient-poor sand the plant grew fewer leaves. (c) 3 / 6 = one half of Pot 1's new leaves. (d) The sunny verandah, with the daily watering that can be carried there. Pot 2 (dark, rich soil, watered) grew no new leaves, because plants need sunlight to make food; Pot 4 (sunny, poor sand, watered) still grew 3 leaves. Poor soil slows growth, but darkness stops it, so sunlight matters more here.
s: Part (a): Pots 1 and 2
Part (b): soil provides nutrients for growth
Part (c): one half
Part (d): the verandah; Pot 2 shows no growth without light, Pot 4 shows some growth in poor soil

questions.q:
A student counts 300 organisms of all kinds in a pond and says: 'Adding the water, soil and sunlight makes the pond's ecosystem 300 + 3, that is 303 items.'
(a) What does the pond's ecosystem include that its community does not?
(b) Why is simple addition the wrong way to describe an ecosystem?
questions.a: (a) The abiotic components (water, soil, air, sunlight, temperature) and the interactions between them and the living beings. (b) An ecosystem is formed by the interaction of the biotic and abiotic components, not by a head-count; the community is the living part and the ecosystem is that community interacting with its surroundings.
s: Part (a): abiotic components and the interactions
Part (b): an ecosystem is formed by interaction, not a count of items

questions.q: True or False? 'A river and the farmland along its banks are two different ecosystems that overlap and interact with each other.' Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: True. The river is an aquatic ecosystem and the farmland is a terrestrial, human-made ecosystem. Ecosystems can overlap: in one area a river can run alongside forests, grassland and farmland, and these ecosystems interact, for example the river's water is used by the crops.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: river aquatic, farmland terrestrial (human-made); ecosystems overlap and interact, e.g. river water for crops

questions.q: A student says a single large mango tree can be called an ecosystem. Support her with three points: two biotic components, two abiotic components, and one interaction between them.
questions.a: Biotic components: the mango tree itself and the birds, ants or squirrels living on it (any two). Abiotic components: sunlight, air, water and the soil in which it grows (any two). Interaction: the tree uses sunlight, carbon dioxide and water to make food, or birds shelter in its branches; biotic and abiotic components interact, so the tree is a small terrestrial ecosystem.
s: Two biotic components
Two abiotic components
One interaction, so it is a (small terrestrial) ecosystem

questions.q:
At noon, students measure the temperature at ground level under a large banyan tree in a park and on a bare paved yard beside it: 27 degrees C and 35 degrees C (illustrative).
(a) How many degrees cooler is it under the tree?
(b) Which influence of plants on abiotic components, named in the chapter, explains this?
questions.a: (a) 35 - 27 = 8 degrees C cooler. (b) Plants help cool the atmosphere (and retain soil moisture), so a biotic component, the tree, influences an abiotic one, the temperature.
s: Part (a): 8 degrees C
Part (b): plants help cool the atmosphere

questions.q:
The chapter sorts interactions by what they influence.
(a) 'Strong sunlight raises the temperature of a shallow rock pool.' Which kind of interaction is this, and what does it influence?
(b) 'A fish takes in oxygen from the water.' Which kind of interaction is this, and which life process does it influence?
questions.a: (a) An interaction between two abiotic components (sunlight and water); it influences the physical characteristics of the habitat, here its temperature. (b) An interaction between a biotic and an abiotic component; it influences respiration.
s: Part (a): abiotic-abiotic; physical characteristics of the habitat
Part (b): biotic-abiotic; respiration

questions.q:
Match each observation in Column I with the description in Column II.
Column I | Column II
1. A stream flows through the middle of a wheat farm | a. An abiotic component supports a life process of an organism
2. Bright sun dries the puddles on a playground by noon | b. Two abiotic components interact
3. A heron catches frogs at the edge of a pond | c. Organisms interact with each other
4. A turtle lays its eggs in the warm sand of a riverbank | d. Two ecosystems overlap

At a lake, students note four observations: (i) a kingfisher catches a fish; (ii) wind ruffles the surface of the lake; (iii) frogs and fish both feed on midge larvae; (iv) a turtle basks on a warm rock. The number of these that are interactions among biotic components is ___.

With their teacher, Class 8 students walked around a lake near Bhopal and wrote down what they saw.
1. Lotus leaves spread over the shallow water.
2. A cormorant dives and catches a fish.
3. The afternoon sun warms the surface water.
4. Wind pushes ripples across the lake.
5. Grass roots along the bank hold the soil when it rains.
6. Herons and cormorants feed on the same small fish.
7. Rice plants in the fields beside the lake grow in water drawn from it.
(a) Which observations are interactions between two abiotic components?
(b) Observation 6 is an interaction among biotic components. What does it affect?
(c) What kinds of ecosystem are the lake and the rice fields, and what does observation 7 show about them?
(d) The lake committee plans a walking path. Plan A runs along the water's edge, clears the grass there, costs Rs 2 lakh and gives visitors a close view of the birds. Plan B is set back, leaves a strip of grass at the edge and costs Rs 3 lakh. Last monsoon, the one stretch where the grass had been trampled bare lost a slice of bank into the lake (illustrative). Using the observations, decide which plan is better for the lake and justify.
questions.a: (a) Observations 3 and 4 (sun warming the water; wind making ripples). (b) The availability of a resource, the small fish that both birds need as food: they compete for it. (c) The lake is an aquatic ecosystem; the rice fields are a terrestrial, human-made ecosystem. Observation 7 shows the two ecosystems overlap and interact. (d) Plan B. Observation 5 and the bare stretch show that grass roots hold the bank's soil in rain; Plan A would strip the roots along the whole edge, so the bank would be eroded into the lake each monsoon. Plan B costs Rs 1 lakh more, but it keeps the soil in place and the lake protected.
s: Part (a): observations 3 and 4
Part (b): availability of food fish (competition)
Part (c): aquatic and human-made terrestrial; they overlap and interact
Part (d): Plan B, as grass roots prevent erosion (observation 5, bare stretch), worth the extra cost

questions.q: In a pond study, four populations of 25 individuals each are counted. A student states that the community has 4 populations. How many individuals are in the community, and what must be added to make an ecosystem?
questions.a: 100 individuals; the abiotic components and their interactions
o: 100 individuals; the abiotic components and their interactions
25 individuals; the other populations of the habitat
100 individuals; only the soil and water of the pond
4 individuals; the interactions among biotic components

questions.q:
A forest guide in Madhya Pradesh fills in a table during a nature walk (illustrative).
Organism | Makes its own food | Feeds on plants | Feeds on animals
Sal tree | Yes | - | -
Sambar deer | No | Yes | No
Jungle crow | No | Yes | Yes
Dhole (wild dog) | No | No | Yes
Bracket fungus on a dead log | No | No (feeds on dead wood) | No
(a) Using the chapter's definition of a heterotroph, how many heterotrophs are in the table?
(b) Label the jungle crow and the dhole as herbivore, carnivore or omnivore.
(c) Write a food chain of three organisms using only this table.
(d) Dholes have been seen chasing sambar near a village, and some villagers ask for all the dholes to be taken out of this forest. Using the table, predict what would then happen to the sambar and to young sal trees, and decide whether removing the dholes would be good for the forest.
questions.a: (a) 4: the sambar deer, jungle crow, dhole and bracket fungus, since none of them makes its own food (all except the sal tree). (b) Jungle crow: omnivore (plants and animals). Dhole: carnivore (only animals). (c) For example, sal tree (leaves) -> sambar deer -> dhole; any valid chain from the table earns the mark. (d) Not good for the forest. The dhole eats the sambar, so without dholes the sambar would increase; more sambar would eat more sal leaves and young sal trees, so the forest's plants would suffer. A change in one population would pass down the chain, so the dholes should stay (the villagers' safety can be handled in other ways).
s: Part (a): 4 heterotrophs, as none makes its own food
Part (b): crow omnivore, dhole carnivore
Part (c): a valid chain such as sal -> sambar -> dhole
Part (d): not good; more sambar would eat more young sal

questions.q:
A school group studied a village pond in Odisha with their teacher and drew its food web (illustrative): algae are eaten by tadpoles and by snails; tadpoles are eaten by small fish; snails are eaten by ducks; small fish are eaten by kingfishers and by herons.
(a) Which organism is the producer, and why?
(b) Write every food chain in this web that ends with a kingfisher or a heron.
(c) A disease kills most of the snails. Which animal is hit hardest, and why?
(d) Which single organism's loss would affect every other organism in this web? Justify.
questions.a: (a) The algae: they make their own food by photosynthesis, so they are the producers at the first trophic level. (b) Algae -> tadpoles -> small fish -> kingfisher; algae -> tadpoles -> small fish -> heron. (c) The ducks, because in this web snails are their only food. (d) The algae. Every chain in the web begins with algae: tadpoles and snails eat them directly, and the small fish, kingfishers, herons and ducks depend on them through those animals, so losing the algae would affect all of them.
s: Part (a): algae, which make their own food
Part (b): the two chains through tadpoles and small fish
Part (c): ducks, whose only food here is snails
Part (d): algae, as every chain starts with them

questions.q:
In a dry grassland (illustrative), grass is eaten by grasshoppers, grasshoppers by lizards, lizards by snakes and snakes by hawks. Match each organism with its place in this chain.
Column I | Column II
1. Lizard | a. Fifth trophic level
2. Grasshopper | b. Fourth trophic level
3. Hawk | c. Second trophic level, a herbivore
4. Snake | d. Third trophic level, a small carnivore
In a grassland food web (illustrative), mice are eaten by owls, snakes and hawks. A disease wipes out the owls. Why might the mouse population still not keep rising out of control?
questions.a: Snakes and hawks also feed on mice
o: Snakes and hawks also feed on mice
Mice are producers, so owls were not needed
Mice turn into decomposers and feed on dead owls
Food chains cannot be linked into a food web

questions.q: In a millet field (illustrative), students estimate 2400 millet plants and 80 mice in the chain millet -> mouse -> eagle. For each organism at the second trophic level there are ___ millet plants.
Dev claims: 'A food web shows the feeding links in a real ecosystem more truly than a single food chain does.' Is he right, wrong or partly right? Explain with an example.
questions.a: Right. A food chain shows only one line of 'who eats whom'. In a real ecosystem each organism may be eaten by two or more kinds of organisms, so the chains are interlinked into a network, the food web. For example, mice are eaten by snakes, owls and hawks; a single chain such as grass -> mouse -> owl misses the snake and the hawk, while the web shows all three links.
s: Verdict: right
An organism is eaten by two or more kinds, so chains interlink into a web
A correct example of a link a single chain misses

questions.q: A row in a student's table reads: 'Performs photosynthesis: No. Feeds on plants and plant products: Yes. Feeds on animals: Yes.' Which organism and feeding group fit this row?
questions.a: Bengal fox; omnivore
o: Bengal fox; omnivore
Hare; herbivore
Vulture; carnivore
Mushroom; decomposer

questions.q:
Examine these statements.
Statement 1: Foxes and mice are both organisms that eat plants as well as animals.
Statement 2: Every food chain must end with a large carnivore such as a tiger.
Statement 3: Decomposers are at the first trophic level, because they feed on plant matter.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: Statement 1 only
o: Statement 1 only
Statements 1 and 2 only
Statements 1 and 3 only
Statements 2 and 3 only

questions.q:
A student says: 'Algae in a pond cannot be producers, because only big green plants like trees make food.'
(a) Is she right? Use what the chapter says about plants such as algae and about how producers make food.
(b) If all the algae of a pond died, which group of organisms in the pond would be hit first, and why?
questions.a: (a) No. The chapter lists algae among the plants of a pond, and plants make their own food by photosynthesis, so they are producers (autotrophs); size does not matter. (b) The animals that feed on the algae, because the producers are the first trophic level and the food of the consumers above them.
s: Part (a): algae are plants that make food by photosynthesis, so producers
Part (b): the animals that eat algae lose their food first

questions.q:
In a village pond (illustrative), students estimate 600 algae clumps, 120 tadpoles, 12 small fish and 2 kingfishers in the chain algae -> tadpoles -> small fish -> kingfisher.
(a) How many algae clumps are there for each tadpole, and how many tadpoles for each small fish?
(b) Stack the four numbers with the largest at the base: which organism is at the top, and at which trophic level is it?
questions.a: (a) 600 / 120 = 5 clumps per tadpole; 120 / 12 = 10 tadpoles per small fish. (b) The kingfisher (2) is at the top, at the fourth trophic level (producer first, then tadpole, small fish, kingfisher); the numbers get smaller at each level and make a pyramid.
s: Part (a): 5 and 10
Part (b): kingfisher at the top, fourth trophic level

questions.a: (a) 5 chains: grass-grasshopper-frog-snake-hawk; grass-grasshopper-bird-hawk; grass-mouse-snake-hawk; grass-mouse-hawk; grass-hare-hawk. (b) Grass -> grasshopper -> frog -> snake -> hawk (five organisms). (c) The hawk is at the third level (grass-mouse-hawk, grass-hare-hawk), the fourth level (through the bird or through mouse and snake) and the fifth level (through frog and snake).
s: Part (a): 5 chains
Part (b): grass -> grasshopper -> frog -> snake -> hawk
Part (c): third, fourth and fifth levels

questions.q: Take an organism's trophic level to be its position in a food chain, counting the producer as the first level. True or False? 'A crow can be at different trophic levels in different food chains.' Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: True. A crow is an omnivore. When it eats grain (a producer), it is at the second trophic level, like a herbivore. When it eats insects that feed on plants, it is at the third trophic level, like a small carnivore. Its level depends on what it eats in that chain.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: as an omnivore it is second level when eating grain and third level when eating plant-eating insects

questions.q:
A student's poster on 'Who eats whom' contains five statements. Find the error in each and correct it.
(1) 'A tree and a leopard are at the same trophic level because both live in the forest.'
(2) 'The crow is a herbivore because it eats grain.'
(3) 'The vulture is at the second trophic level.'
(4) 'Food chains in an ecosystem stay separate from one another.'
(5) 'Decomposers are not part of an ecosystem because they eat only dead things.'
questions.a: (1) Trophic level is a position in a food chain, not a place: green plants (producers) are at the first level and a leopard, a carnivore, is at a higher level. (2) The crow also eats animals such as insects, so it is an omnivore, not a herbivore. (3) The vulture is a large carnivore, so it is above the herbivores (second level); in a chain such as grass -> hare -> vulture it is at least at the third level, never the second. (4) Each organism may be eaten by two or more kinds, so chains are interlinked into a food web. (5) Decomposers such as fungi and bacteria are part of every ecosystem: they break down dead matter and return nutrients to the soil for plants.
s: (1) trophic level is a position: producers first, leopard higher
(2) crow is an omnivore
(3) vulture is a carnivore above the second level
(4) chains interlink into a food web
(5) decomposers are part of the ecosystem and recycle nutrients

questions.q:
A student lists eight organisms: mango tree, goat, tiger, crow, bacteria, grass, mushroom and hare.
(a) How many are producers, how many herbivores, how many decomposers, and which single organism is an omnivore?
(b) How many of the eight are heterotrophs?
(c) The bacteria and the mushroom are heterotrophs but not consumers in the chapter's sense. What do they do that a goat or a tiger does not?
questions.a: (a) Producers: mango tree and grass = 2; herbivores: goat and hare = 2; decomposers: bacteria and mushroom = 2; the crow is the omnivore (the tiger is a carnivore). (b) 6: every organism except the mango tree and the grass, since none of those six makes its own food. (c) They break down the complex substances in dead plants and animals into simpler ones and return nutrients to the soil, instead of eating living organisms.
s: Part (a): 2 producers, 2 herbivores, 2 decomposers; crow omnivore
Part (b): 6 heterotrophs
Part (c): decomposers break down dead matter and return nutrients to the soil

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Mushrooms growing on a dead log are producers, like the tree whose wood they grow on.
Reason (R): Fungi break down complex substances in dead plants and animals into simpler ones.
questions.a: A is false, but R is true
o: A is false, but R is true
A is true, but R is false
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A

questions.q: 'Decomposers are as important to an ecosystem as producers.' Justify this statement in five points.
questions.a: (1) Producers make food by photosynthesis, using sunlight, water, carbon dioxide and nutrients from the soil. (2) Organisms produce a lot of waste during their lives, and they die; this dead matter and waste would otherwise pile up. (3) Decomposers such as fungi and bacteria break down the complex substances in dead plants and animals into simpler ones. (4) This returns important nutrients to the soil; many of the nutrients in soil come from decomposition. (5) Without decomposers, producers would slowly lack the nutrients they need, and so would every consumer that depends on them; nature reuses everything only because decomposers recycle it. So both are needed.
s: Producers need soil nutrients to grow
Living things produce waste and die
Decomposers break complex dead matter into simpler substances
Nutrients are returned to the soil
Without them producers and consumers would suffer; both are essential

questions.q: A student writes a 'food chain' for a forest: deer -> tiger. Show that a food chain cannot begin with the deer, and correct the chain.
questions.a: A deer is a herbivore: it cannot make its own food and depends on plants for it, so it is a heterotroph (consumer). Only producers, the green plants that make food by photosynthesis, can stand at the first trophic level, because every consumer's food traces back to them. So the chain must start with a plant: grass (or leaves) -> deer -> tiger.
s: Deer is a heterotroph that depends on plants for food
The first trophic level must be a producer that makes its own food
Corrected chain: grass -> deer -> tiger

questions.q:
(a) 'Every herbivore is a heterotroph, but not every heterotroph is a herbivore.' Explain this sentence with examples.
(b) Is every heterotroph an animal that eats living plants or animals? Use the mushroom to answer.
questions.a: (a) A herbivore such as a deer cannot make its own food and depends on plants, so it is a heterotroph. But carnivores (leopard) and omnivores (crow, fox, mouse) are also heterotrophs without being herbivores. (b) No. A mushroom cannot make its own food, so it is a heterotroph, but it feeds on dead matter, breaking it down, so it is a saprotroph (decomposer), not an eater of living things.
s: Part (a): herbivores are heterotrophs; carnivores and omnivores are heterotrophs too
Part (b): no; the mushroom is a heterotroph that feeds on dead matter (saprotroph)

questions.q: A student says a mushroom on a fallen log and a mouse in a field are both consumers because neither makes its own food. Which point from the chapter shows what the mushroom does that the mouse does not?
questions.a: It breaks dead matter into simpler substances and returns nutrients to the soil
o: It breaks dead matter into simpler substances and returns nutrients to the soil
It makes its own food from sunlight, carbon dioxide and water
It eats living plants only and so sits at the second trophic level
It eats both plants and animals and so is an omnivore

questions.q: In a crop field, millet is eaten by mice, mice by snakes and snakes by eagles. A disease kills most of the mice (illustrative). Which change comes first?
questions.a: Snakes, which eat mice, have less food
o: Snakes, which eat mice, have less food
Millet has less food, as mice used to feed it
Eagles lose food first, as they eat mice directly
Snakes have more food, as dead mice are easy prey

questions.q:
Beetles and flies gather on fresh elephant dung in a forest.
(a) Which role in nature are they playing here?
(b) Suppose the dung beetles disappeared from this forest (illustrative). Predict one change in the dung and one change in the soil.
questions.a: (a) They help break the dung down and recycle its nutrients, so they take part in decomposition. (b) The dung would break down more slowly and pile up, and fewer nutrients would be returned to the soil for plants.
s: Part (a): help break down dung and recycle nutrients (decomposition)
Part (b): dung piles up; fewer nutrients return to the soil

questions.q: In a paddy field, rice plants are eaten by grasshoppers, grasshoppers by frogs, frogs by snakes and snakes by eagles. Mohan says the frog is at the second trophic level because it is the second animal in the chain. At which trophic level is the frog?
questions.a: The third trophic level
o: The third trophic level
The second trophic level
The fourth trophic level
The first trophic level

questions.q:
A Class 8 group lists five pairs it saw on a nature walk with its teacher. For each pair, name the kind of interaction and say what each partner gains or loses.
(1) A butterfly sipping nectar from a marigold and carrying its pollen to the next flower
(2) A fern growing on the trunk of a healthy mango tree, using it only for support
(3) A leech feeding on the blood of a buffalo in a pond
(4) Two saplings growing towards the same small gap of sunlight in a forest
(5) A leopard hunting a wild boar
questions.a: (1) Mutualism: the butterfly gets nectar and the marigold gets pollinated; both benefit. (2) Commensalism: the fern gets physical support; the tree is not affected. (3) Parasitism: the leech benefits by feeding on blood; the buffalo is harmed. (4) Competition for a common resource, sunlight; whichever sapling gets less light grows poorly, and this competition helps control population size. (5) A predator-prey (feeding) relationship: the leopard gets food and the wild boar is killed; predators rely on a healthy prey population.
s: (1) mutualism, both benefit
(2) commensalism, tree unaffected
(3) parasitism, buffalo harmed
(4) competition for sunlight
(5) predator and prey; leopard relies on prey

questions.q:
A tiger reserve in central India (illustrative figures) kept this record. Between 2018 and 2022, grazing by village cattle inside the reserve was stopped, and grassland was allowed to regrow.
Year | Deer and wild boar (per sq km) | Tigers in the reserve
2010 | 50 | 30
2014 | 38 | 26
2018 | 22 | 17
2022 | 41 | 28
(a) What is the relationship between the tigers and the deer and wild boar, and which population relies on the other?
(b) By what percentage did the prey density fall from 2010 to 2018, and how did the tigers change over the same years?
(c) Which finding of A.J.T. Johnsingh does this record agree with?
(d) Nearby villages ask to graze their cattle in the reserve again; the reserve would earn grazing fees and the villagers more milk income. Should the reserve allow it? Decide, using the record.
questions.a: (a) Predator and prey: the tigers hunt the deer and wild boar, so the tiger population relies on the prey population. (b) (50 - 22) / 50 x 100 = 56%; over the same years the tigers fell from 30 to 17. (c) Predators such as tigers rely on prey such as deer and wild boar; a healthy prey population is key to predator survival. (d) No. The record shows the prey recovered (22 to 41) only after cattle grazing was stopped and the grassland regrew, and the tigers followed (17 to 28). Allowing grazing again would bring back the conditions of 2010-2018, when prey and then tigers fell, so the fees and milk income would come at the cost of the tigers.
s: Part (a): predator and prey; tigers rely on prey
Part (b): 56%; tigers fell from 30 to 17
Part (c): healthy prey is key to predator survival
Part (d): no; prey and tigers recovered only after grazing stopped

questions.q: In a forest like Bandipur (illustrative), a disease sharply reduces the deer and wild boar. Based on what A.J.T. Johnsingh found, what should be expected for the tigers and leopards there?
questions.a: They will struggle, as healthy prey is key to survival
o: They will struggle, as healthy prey is key to survival
They will be unaffected, as predators do not rely on prey
They will multiply, as prey no longer compete with them
They will become decomposers and feed on the dead prey

questions.q: Four pairs of organisms are described. Which pair shows commensalism?
questions.a: A fern growing on a healthy tree trunk, using it only for support
o: A fern growing on a healthy tree trunk, using it only for support
A sunbird sipping nectar while carrying pollen between flowers
A tick feeding on the blood of a dog that keeps scratching
Two saplings growing towards the same gap of sunlight

questions.q: A chain of events in an ecosystem ends like this: '...so the farmers were forced to spray more pesticide.' Write at least three earlier links that could lead to this ending. Use ideas from the chapter, but do NOT use the frog-leg example or the polluted-pond example.
questions.a: Sample answer: A farmer clears the hedges and bushes around his fields, where beetles and birds that feed on pests used to live. With fewer of these natural predators, the pest population increases. The pests damage the crop, so the farmers are forced to spray more pesticide. (Another valid chain: an old tree where insect-eating bats roosted is cut, the bats leave, insects increase and damage crops.) Any chain of three or more correct cause-and-effect links that ends with more pesticide use earns the marks.
s: A first change that removes or harms a pest-eater
A correct middle link (fewer predators, so more pests)
Pests damage crops, so more spraying

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Banning the export of frog legs helped limit the use of synthetic pesticides on India's farms.
Reason (R): Frogs eat insects, so protecting them keeps farm pests in check.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true

questions.q: Vikram claims: 'In the 1980s frog-leg story, the farmers were to blame for the harm to soil and water, not the loss of frogs.' Is he right, wrong or partly right? Explain.
questions.a: Wrong. The chain began with the large-scale harvesting of frogs for export, which reduced frog populations. Since frogs eat insects, agricultural pests rose, and this forced farmers to use more synthetic pesticides, which harmed the soil, water and health. The loss of frogs was the cause of the extra spraying, which is why the Government of India banned the export of frog legs.
s: Verdict: wrong
Harvesting frogs reduced them, so pests rose
Rising pests forced the extra pesticide use; hence the export ban

questions.q: True or False? 'A balanced ecosystem is one in which the number of each kind of organism never changes.' Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: False. An ecosystem is in balance when interactions among organisms and their environment keep populations and resources stable, but this balance is dynamic, not fixed. Populations rise and fall and are kept in check (for example, by competition), and natural or human-made changes can disturb the balance.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: the balance is dynamic, not fixed; numbers change but are kept in check

questions.q: Pollution kills many of the plants in a pond. Soon the fish begin to die, even though they still have plenty of small animals to eat. The fish are most likely short of ___.
questions.a: oxygen

questions.q: Frogs and fish in a village pond both feed on the same small insect larvae. After a long dry spell the larvae become scarce. Going by the chapter, what is most likely?
questions.a: Competition between the frogs and fish for the larvae grows stronger
o: Competition between the frogs and fish for the larvae grows stronger
The frogs and fish turn into mutualists and share the larvae
The frogs become parasites of the fish to get food
The fish are unaffected, as commensalism protects them

questions.q:
In a village, bats that feed on insects at night roost in an old banyan tree beside the fields (illustrative). The tree is cut down for a road, and the bats leave.
(a) Which change does cutting the tree cause directly?
(b) Trace how this could end up affecting the farmers' crops.
questions.a: (a) The bats lose their roost and leave the village, so there are fewer bats. (b) With fewer bats eating them, more insects survive; more insects can damage the crops, and farmers may then have to use more pesticide. One change passes on to others through the feeding link.
s: Part (a): bats lose their roost, so fewer bats
Part (b): fewer bats, more insects, more crop damage (and pesticide)

questions.a: (a) (i) Mutualism; (ii) commensalism; (iii) parasitism. (b) Observation (iv): the birds compete for a common resource (food), and competition helps control population size. (c) The tick benefits by feeding on the dog's blood; the dog is harmed, getting skin irritation (it keeps scratching). (d) Plan A, the beehives without spray. Observation (i) is mutualism: the bees pollinate the flowers, and pollination is needed for seeds to form. With hives, about 80 of every 100 flowers set seed and 10% of the crop is lost to leaf-eaters, leaving 80 x 0.9 = 72 units; with the spray the bees are killed too, so only 35 flowers in 100 set seed, which is 35 units even though no leaves are lost. The spray costs more seed than it saves.
s: Part (a): mutualism, commensalism, parasitism
Part (b): (iv), competition
Part (c): tick benefits from blood; dog harmed by irritation
Part (d): beehives; bees pollinate the flowers, and a spray during flowering would kill them

questions.q:
Waste from a small factory starts flowing into a village pond near Kanpur. Volunteers record the pond and the farm beside it (illustrative figures).
Month | Pond surface covered by plants (%) | Fish caught in 5 net hauls | Insects in a light trap at the farm (one night) | Pesticide sprays that month
January | 70 | 40 | 120 | 1
April | 45 | 26 | 210 | 2
July | 20 | 9 | 390 | 4
(a) Which change shown in the record comes first in the chain of events?
(b) Explain the link between the dying plants and the falling fish catch.
(c) How many times as many insects were trapped in July as in January?
(d) For the next three years the farmers can afford one plan. Plan 1: spray pesticide every week, which protects this season's crop at once. Plan 2: join the volunteers in getting the factory waste stopped and replanting the pond, which takes a season or two to work. Which plan should they choose? Justify using the trend in the record and the chain.
questions.a: (a) The pond plants dying (plant cover falling from 70% to 20%) after the waste enters. (b) With fewer plants, less oxygen is produced in the water, so the fish population drops. (c) 390 / 120 = 3.25 times. (d) Plan 2. The record shows the sprays already doubling (1, 2, 4) while the insects still more than tripled, because the cause upstream is getting worse: the waste kills plants, so less oxygen, fewer fish and more insects. Weekly spraying treats only the last link, would have to keep growing and may harm the environment further; stopping the waste lets plants, oxygen and fish recover, so over three years it protects the crop better.
s: Part (a): the plants dying
Part (b): fewer plants, less oxygen, fewer fish
Part (c): 3.25 times
Part (d): Plan 2; sprays are rising yet insects keep rising, so only removing the cause works over three years

questions.q: A student collects examples of competition for a common resource. Which example does NOT belong in her list?
questions.a: A tick sucking blood from a dog
o: A tick sucking blood from a dog
Two saplings growing towards one gap of sunlight
Two kinds of birds feeding on the same figs
Deer and hares grazing on the same grass

questions.q: Sana claims: 'An orchid growing on a tree is a parasite, because it lives on another plant and the tree is harmed a little by carrying it.' Is she right, wrong or partly right? Explain.
questions.a: Partly right. She is right that the orchid lives on the tree. She is wrong that this makes it a parasite: in parasitism one organism benefits and the other is harmed, as ticks feed on a dog's blood. The book describes the orchid as getting physical support while the tree branch is unaffected, so the relationship is commensalism, and no harm to the tree is described.
s: Verdict: partly right
Right part: the orchid lives on the tree
Wrong part: parasitism needs harm; the orchid only gets support and the tree is unaffected (commensalism)

questions.q:
A small grassy island (illustrative) has deer but no other grazing animals and no predators. Rangers recorded:
Year | Deer | Island covered by grass (%)
2010 | 20 | 90
2013 | 60 | 70
2016 | 180 | 15
2019 | 40 | 10
Analyse the record in five points: (1) by what factor the deer multiplied in each three-year period up to 2016, (2) why they could multiply so fast here, (3) what happened to the grass and why, (4) by what percentage the deer fell from 2016 to 2019, and why, (5) what this shows about competition and balance, as described in the chapter.
questions.a: (1) 60 / 20 = 3 and 180 / 60 = 3, so the deer tripled every three years. (2) No other grazers competed with them for the grass and no predators ate them, so nothing kept their numbers in check. (3) Grass cover fell from 90% to 15% because more and more deer ate it. (4) (180 - 40) / 180 x 100 is about 78%; with little grass left, food became scarce and most deer could not survive. (5) The chapter says competition helps control population size and keeps the ecosystem balanced; without it, one species can multiply too much and cause an imbalance, as happened here.
s: (1) tripled each period (factor 3)
(2) no competitors or predators to keep numbers in check
(3) grass fell from 90% to 15% as deer ate it
(4) about 78% fall, as food became scarce
(5) without competition one species multiplies too much: imbalance

questions.q:
A student sows the same kind of seed in three pots of equal size and soil (illustrative): 1, 5 and 20 seeds per pot. After four weeks the average height of the seedlings is 24 cm, 19 cm and 9 cm.
(a) By what percentage is the seedling in the 20-seed pot shorter than the one in the 1-seed pot?
(b) Name the interaction that explains the trend, and say how it keeps populations in check.
questions.a: (a) (24 - 9) / 24 x 100 = 62.5%. (b) Competition for common resources such as water, food (nutrients), space and sunlight; the more seedlings share a pot, the less each gets, and competition helps control population size so that one species does not multiply too much.
s: Part (b): competition for resources; it controls population size

questions.q:
Honeybees visit the flowers of a mustard field in Rajasthan.
(a) What does each partner get from the visits, and what is the relationship called?
(b) Suppose a disease wiped out the honeybees around the field (illustrative). Predict the effect on the mustard seed harvest and give the reason.
questions.a: (a) The bee gets nectar and the flower gets pollinated; both benefit, so it is mutualism. (b) Fewer flowers would be pollinated, and pollination is needed for fruits and seeds to form, so the seed harvest would fall.
s: Part (a): bee gets nectar, flower gets pollinated; mutualism
Part (b): less pollination, so fewer seeds

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about balance in ecosystems.
Statement 1: The balance of an ecosystem can be upset by natural changes as well as by human-made ones.
Statement 2: A change in one population can pass on to other populations through feeding links.
Statement 3: In commensalism, both organisms are harmed a little.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: Statements 1 and 2 only
o: Statements 1 and 2 only
Statements 2 and 3 only
Statement 2 only
All three statements

questions.q:
Take this rule from the chapter: an ecosystem is in balance when its interactions keep populations stable around a level, even though the numbers may rise and fall; it is out of balance when a population keeps running away in one direction. A lake's fish were counted every six months (illustrative): 120, 150, 135, 125.
(a) A visitor says the lake must be out of balance because the number keeps changing. Is that a sound conclusion?
(b) Explain your answer using the rule.
questions.a: (a) No. A changing count alone does not prove imbalance. (b) By the rule, balance allows numbers to rise and fall; here the count went up and came back down towards where it started (120, then 150, 135, 125), so it is staying around a level rather than running away in one direction. Balance is dynamic, not fixed.
s: Part (a): not sound; change alone does not prove imbalance
Part (b): the count rises and returns towards its level, so by the rule it is in dynamic balance

questions.q: The chapter says an ecosystem's balance can be disturbed by natural or by human-made changes. Which of these is a natural change that could disturb a pond's balance?
questions.a: A long drought that dries up most of the pond
o: A long drought that dries up most of the pond
Factory waste flowing into the pond every day
Netting almost all the fish out of the pond
Pesticide from nearby fields washing into it

questions.q: True or False? 'Synthetic fertilisers have only ever harmed India's soil and never helped its food supply.' Give the verdict and the reason or correction.
questions.a: False. Synthetic fertilisers and pesticides played a vital role in raising crop production and helped India become food secure after the food crisis of 1950-1965. The harm comes from their overuse over a long time, which can lower soil fertility by reducing friendly microorganisms and humus.
s: Verdict: False
Correction: they helped make India food secure; the harm comes from long-term overuse

questions.q: Villagers dig a fish pond and stock it once, then leave it untended for years (illustrative). Considering what the chapter says about human-made ecosystems, what is the most likely result?
questions.a: It may degrade, since human-made ecosystems need care and management
o: It may degrade, since human-made ecosystems need care and management
It stays healthy, since every ecosystem looks after itself
It turns into a natural ecosystem, since people stopped working
It supports more biodiversity, since people left it alone

questions.q:
Two neighbouring farms near Ludhiana (illustrative figures) were compared over ten years. Farm X uses compost and little synthetic fertiliser and grows three different crops. Farm Y uses heavy synthetic fertiliser and grows only wheat every year.
Measure | Farm X | Farm Y
Wheat yield in year 1 (quintals per acre) | 17 | 25
Wheat yield in year 10 (quintals per acre) | 18 | 21
Earthworms per spadeful of soil in year 10 | 14 | 3
Humus in the soil in year 10 (%) | 2.4 | 0.9
Pesticide sprays per season in year 10 | 1 | 5
(a) By what percentage did Farm Y's yield fall from year 1 to year 10?
(b) Using the chapter, explain why Farm Y has so little humus and needs five sprays a season.
(c) Farm Y still has the higher yield in year 10. Does that show its methods are better for the land? Use two rows of the table.
(d) A young farmer is taking over Farm Y for the next thirty years. Assuming each farm's yield keeps changing at the same steady rate per year as over years 1 to 10, should she move towards Farm X's methods? Decide and justify using the yield trends and the soil rows.
questions.a: (a) (25 - 21) / 25 x 100 = 16%. (b) Overusing synthetic fertiliser lowers friendly microorganisms and humus; it also reduces natural predators, so pests increase, and repeated spraying can make pests resistant, so more sprays are needed. (c) No. Its soil has only 3 earthworms per spadeful against 14 and 0.9% humus against 2.4%; the soil life and organic matter that keep land fertile are being lost. (d) Yes. Y's yield falls by 4/9 (about 0.44) quintal a year while X's rises by 1/9 (about 0.11); the two lines meet after about 14 years (about 5 years after year 10), and over thirty years Y would end well below X. Y's low humus (0.9% against 2.4%) and few earthworms (3 against 14) also leave its soil prone to erosion, so moving to compost and more than one crop is the better choice for the next thirty years even though Y is ahead today.
s: Part (a): 16%
Part (b): fertiliser overuse cuts microbes, humus and natural predators; pests rise or resist
Part (c): no; earthworms and humus figures show soil damage
Part (d): yes; Y falls about 0.44 a year, X rises about 0.11, they meet after about 14 years, and Y's soil is degrading

questions.q:
A survey of one island in the Indian Sundarbans (illustrative figures) found that its mangrove cover fell from 38 sq km in 2005 to 29 sq km in 2025, mostly where trees were cut for fuelwood and for new farm plots. In the last cyclone, 8% of the houses on the island's mangrove-lined east side were damaged, against 35% on the cleared west side.
(a) What percentage of the island's mangrove cover was lost from 2005 to 2025?
(b) Explain, using the chapter, why the west side suffered so much more damage.
(c) A grant can pay to replant mangroves on one side of the island first. Which side should be replanted first, and which threat named in the chapter must also be tackled so that the new mangroves survive? Justify.
questions.a: (a) (38 - 29) / 38 x 100, which is about 23.7% (roughly 24%). (b) Mangroves slow down strong winds and waves during storms and floods. The east side still has its mangrove belt, so less of the storm's force reached the houses; on the cleared west side nothing slowed the wind and waves, so more than four times as many houses were damaged (35% against 8%). (c) The west side, where the mangroves were cut and the damage was greatest. The cutting of mangroves for fuelwood and farming must also be tackled, otherwise the new trees will be cut down again.
s: Part (a): about 23.7%
Part (b): mangroves slow wind and waves; the cleared side had no such belt
Part (c): replant the west side first and stop cutting for fuelwood and farming

questions.q: In a Punjab village, the tube wells that water the rice fields have to be dug deeper almost every year (illustrative). Which reason the chapter gives for calling Green Revolution methods unsustainable does this show?
questions.a: Excessive groundwater extraction
o: Excessive groundwater extraction
Overuse of synthetic fertilisers
Growing only one type of crop
Use of tractors and machines

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The Sundarbans protect people living near the coast during storms and floods.
Reason (R): UNESCO declared the Sundarbans a World Heritage Site in 1987.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true

questions.q: Chilika Lake in Odisha is one of India's protected areas. What kind of ecosystem is it mainly, and what does protecting it achieve?
questions.a: Aquatic; it conserves whole habitats and their wildlife
o: Aquatic; it conserves whole habitats and their wildlife
Terrestrial; it conserves the farms along its shore
Aquatic; it lets the lake be fished without any limit
Human-made; it needs no further care once it is set aside

questions.q: A town plans to turn an old stone quarry into a human-made ecosystem: a fish pond surrounded by a park. Suggest three conditions, based on the chapter, that the plan must meet if the new ecosystem is to help the town rather than become a problem.
questions.a: Sample answer. (1) It must be well designed so that it reduces pollution, for example the pond should not receive sewage or waste. (2) It should support biodiversity, with many kinds of plants and animals, not just one crop or one kind of fish. (3) It must have people and money for its continued care and management, since, unlike a natural ecosystem, a human-made one does not look after itself. It can also give the town a recreational space.
s: Designed to reduce pollution
Supports biodiversity
Has continued human care and management

questions.q: A village switches every field to a single commercial crop for ten years. Orchard owners nearby notice fewer visiting bees and poorer fruit set (illustrative). Which point from the chapter explains this?
questions.a: Monoculture reduces biodiversity and affects pollinators
o: Monoculture reduces biodiversity and affects pollinators
Heavy ploughing disturbs earthworms and snails
Some pests develop resistance to pesticides
Low humus leaves soil prone to erosion

questions.q:
Match each farm observation in Column I with the chapter's most likely explanation in Column II.
Column I | Column II
1. Rain washes soil off a field that has had heavy fertiliser for years | a. Disturbed soil organisms such as earthworms and snails
2. Earthworms are rare in a field ploughed six times a year and flooded weekly | b. Less humus to bind soil particles
3. A pesticide that once killed most pests now kills only a few | c. Pests have developed resistance
4. Bees are scarce around fields that grow one crop year after year | d. Monoculture has reduced biodiversity and affected pollinators

A cotton farmer records the share of pests killed by the same pesticide dose in four successive seasons (illustrative): 95%, 80%, 55%, 30%. What does the trend most likely show, according to the chapter?
questions.a: Some pests have become resistant to the pesticide
o: Some pests have become resistant to the pesticide
The cotton plants have become resistant to the pesticide
The pesticide is turning into a natural predator
Earthworms are breaking the pesticide down

questions.q:
A company offers a village Rs 50 lakh to cut down its forest for timber (illustrative).
(a) Name three benefits of the forest, other than timber, that the village would lose.
(b) Why might the village be worse off in the long run even after the payment?
questions.a: (a) Any three of fresh air, fertile soil, food, fibres, medicines, and aesthetic or recreational value. (b) The money is paid once, but the forest's benefits come every year; misusing the resource disturbs the balance in nature, so the village loses fresh air, soil and food for good (and, as the chapter shows with the elephants, animals that lose their habitat may move into the village).
s: Part (a): three non-timber benefits
Part (b): one-time money against lasting benefits; balance disturbed

questions.q: Farida claims: 'Overusing synthetic fertiliser on a farm can end up increasing the pests there.' Is she right, wrong or partly right? Explain.
questions.a: Right. The chapter says the overuse of synthetic fertilisers reduces the population of natural predators (such as beetles that feed on pests), which ultimately increases the population of pests. It also lowers friendly soil microbes and humus, weakening the soil, so the farm loses natural pest control and soil health together.
s: Verdict: right
Overuse reduces natural predators of pests
Fewer predators means more pests (beetles feed on pests)

questions.q:
Read the statements.
Statement 1: Human-made ecosystems such as fish ponds look after themselves once they are set up.
Statement 2: The Sundarbans lie where the Ganges and Brahmaputra rivers meet, between India and Bangladesh.
Statement 3: Green Revolution methods are now called unsustainable only because they used tractors and machines.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: Statement 2 only
o: Statement 2 only
Statements 1 and 2 only
Statements 2 and 3 only
Statement 3 only

questions.q:
Kunapa Jala, praised in the ancient text Vrikshayurveda, is a liquid fertiliser made by fermenting animal and plant waste.
(a) Which process studied earlier in this chapter does this fermentation resemble, and why?
(b) Why could a farmer who uses such organic manure regularly depend less on synthetic fertiliser?
questions.a: (a) Decomposition: fermentation breaks the complex substances in the waste into simpler ones, just as decomposers break down dead matter. (b) The manure keeps returning nutrients and organic matter to the soil, continuously nourishing it and keeping it healthy, so less synthetic fertiliser is needed.
s: Part (a): decomposition, since complex substances are broken into simpler ones
Part (b): it nourishes the soil with nutrients and organic matter, so less synthetic fertiliser is needed

questions.q: After years of heavy fertiliser, the humus in a field falls from 2.5% to 0.8% (illustrative). The percentage of the original humus that is left is ___.

Two fields on one farm were sampled (illustrative). Field P is ploughed once a year and watered as the crop needs; Field Q is ploughed six times a year and flooded every week. Field P has 12 earthworms per spadeful of soil; Field Q has 4.
(a) How many times as many earthworms does Field P have as Field Q?
(b) Use the chapter to explain the difference, and say which field a farmer should choose for a crop whose roots need loose, living soil.
questions.a: (a) 12 / 4 = 3 times. (b) Heavy irrigation and repeated ploughing disturb soil organisms such as earthworms and snails, so Field Q has fewer. These organisms are important for maintaining ecological balance, so Field Q's soil life and balance are being harmed. Field P should be chosen: its soil organisms are less disturbed.
s: Part (a): 3 times
Part (b): heavy irrigation and ploughing disturb earthworms, which keep the balance

questions.q: Raghav claims: 'Growing one crop on the same land every year is harmless as long as the yield stays high.' Is he right, wrong or partly right? Explain.
questions.a: Wrong. Growing the same crop repeatedly (monoculture) can reduce biodiversity and affect pollinators, which are crucial for food production. Many scientists also believe that growing the same crop repeatedly on the same land, along with overusing pesticides, leads to soil degradation, so a high yield now does not mean no harm.
s: Verdict: wrong
Monoculture reduces biodiversity and affects pollinators
It contributes to soil degradation, so present yield is not proof of no harm

questions.q: Compare a natural forest ecosystem with a human-made farm ecosystem on five points: (1) who keeps it going, (2) the variety of living things, (3) what happens to its soil when it is managed badly, (4) the benefits each gives people, (5) one way the farm can be made more like a healthy natural ecosystem.
questions.a: (1) A natural forest keeps itself going through the interactions of its organisms and surroundings; a farm needs human care and management. (2) A forest has many kinds of plants, animals and microbes; a farm often has one main crop, and monoculture reduces biodiversity. (3) In a forest, roots hold the soil and decomposers return nutrients; on a badly managed farm, overuse of synthetic fertilisers lowers humus and friendly microbes, so the soil erodes, and heavy ploughing disturbs earthworms. (4) A forest gives fresh air, fertile soil, timber, fibres and medicines; a farm gives food and livelihood. (5) The farm can use organic manure such as compost or Kunapa Jala and reduce synthetic chemicals (organic or natural farming), keeping soil organisms, natural predators and pollinators.
s: (1) self-sustaining versus needs human care
(2) many kinds versus monoculture with less biodiversity
(3) soil held and recycled versus humus loss and erosion
(4) benefits of each
(5) organic manure or natural farming to restore soil life

questions.q: A farmer in Haryana has grown only wheat for years, using heavy synthetic fertiliser and pesticide and flooding his field often. He asks you for a five-step plan to make his farm more sustainable while still growing food. Give five steps, each with the chapter's reason.
questions.a: Sample answer. (1) Add organic manure or compost (for example, a liquid manure like Kunapa Jala) and cut back synthetic fertiliser, because overuse lowers friendly microbes and humus, and humus binds soil and prevents erosion. (2) Grow more than one crop instead of only wheat, because monoculture reduces biodiversity and affects pollinators. (3) Spray pesticide only when needed, because overuse reduces natural predators and some pests become resistant. (4) Water only as the crop needs and plough less, because heavy irrigation and repeated ploughing disturb earthworms and snails, and excessive groundwater extraction is unsustainable. (5) Keep spaces where natural predators such as beetles and pollinators can live, so pests are kept in check and crops are pollinated. Any five steps with correct chapter reasons earn the marks.
s: Organic manure in place of excess fertiliser, with reason
More than one crop, with reason
Less pesticide, with reason
Less flooding and ploughing, with reason
Protect natural predators or pollinators, with reason

questions.q:
India faced a food crisis between 1950 and 1965, and the Green Revolution of the mid-20th century raised food production with tractors, machines, synthetic fertilisers and pesticides.
(a) For how many years did the food crisis last?
(b) A student argues: 'These methods ended the crisis, so they should never be questioned.' Use the chapter to answer her.
questions.a: (a) 1965 - 1950 = 15 years. (b) The methods did raise production and helped India become food secure, but their long-term overuse is now considered unsustainable: overuse of synthetic chemicals, excessive groundwater extraction and growing one crop damage soil and biodiversity, so success in the past does not make the methods safe to continue unchanged.
s: Part (a): 15 years
Part (b): they helped, but long-term overuse harms soil and the environment, so they must be questioned
